title: U.S. time allocation shows work, care, household maintenance, socializing, and digital leisure competing within a fixed daily budget
source_unit: Bureau of Labor Statistics, American Time Use Survey—2025 Results, USDL-26-1022
geography: United States; nationally representative American Time Use Survey estimates for people age 15 and older, with subgroup tables by sex, age, education, employment, and presence of children

observations.period: 2025 ATUS annual averages; work location and education

denominator.unit: approximately interviewed individuals in the 2025 ATUS; estimates are nationally representative

work_at_home.unit: percent of employed people doing some or all work at home on days worked

work_at_workplace.unit: percent of employed people doing some or all work at their workplace on days worked

education_home_work_gap.value: 51% among workers with a bachelor's degree or higher versus 19% among workers with a high school diploma and no college doing some work at home

gender_home_work_gap.value: 38% of employed women versus 31% of employed men doing some work at home

mechanism.value: Remote-work flexibility is a labor-market resource distributed by education and gender, with consequences for how paid work can be combined with care and household tasks

observations.method: BLS annual ATUS estimates based on time diaries, weighted for population and day-of-week representation.
observations.uncertainty: Work location is measured on days worked and does not establish productivity, autonomy, commuting savings, or whether home work increases or reduces total work and care burden.
observations.subgroup: Employed people by sex, education, jobholding status, day of week, and other characteristics.
observations.counterinterpretation: Working at home may provide flexibility for some workers while also increasing work-home boundary erosion, surveillance, or unpaid interruptions for others.

observations.period: 2025 ATUS annual averages; household work and gender

denominator.unit: U.S. civilian population age 15 and older; primary activities on an average day

household_activity_participation.unit: percent engaging in household activities on an average day

women_household_participation.unit: percent of women spending time on household activities on an average day

men_household_participation.unit: percent of men spending time on household activities on an average day

conditional_hours_women.unit: average hours on household activities among women who did them

conditional_hours_men.unit: average hours on household activities among men who did them

mechanism.value: The household remains a production site whose time demands are gendered even when employment and income statistics appear similar

observations.method: BLS primary-activity time-use estimates from 2025 ATUS diaries, with conditional hours among people participating in household activities.
observations.uncertainty: Primary-activity estimates exclude many simultaneous activities; participation and conditional hours do not reveal task intensity, division of labor, outsourcing, or control over household decisions.
observations.subgroup: Women and men age 15 and older, with further subgroup tables by age, education, employment, and household composition.
observations.counterinterpretation: Differences may partly reflect age, household structure, employment, and activity mix rather than gender alone; unpaid work can also produce intrinsic or relational benefits.

observations.period: 2025 ATUS annual averages; socializing, television, and computer leisure compared with 2015

denominator.unit: U.S. civilian population age 15 and older; primary leisure activities on an average day

leisure_participation.unit: percent engaging in some leisure or sports activity on an average day

tv_time.unit: average hours per day watching television

socializing_2025.unit: percent engaging in socializing and communicating on an average day in 2025

socializing_2015.unit: percent engaging in socializing and communicating on an average day in 2015

socializing_minutes.value: 35 minutes in 2025 versus 41 minutes in 2015 among the population average

computer_game_time.value: 37 minutes in 2025 versus 25 minutes in 2015 playing games or using a computer for leisure

mechanism.value: Leisure is not disappearing; its composition is shifting from face-to-face socializing toward screen-based and computer-mediated time

observations.method: BLS comparison of 2025 and 2015 ATUS annual averages for primary leisure activities.
observations.uncertainty: The categories do not capture all simultaneous communication or platform use, and the comparison is descriptive rather than a causal estimate of technology effects on social connection.
observations.subgroup: People age 15 and older, with age and sex differences reported in the ATUS tables.
observations.counterinterpretation: Computer-mediated leisure can include social interaction, games, learning, and creative activity; lower recorded face-to-face socializing does not prove lower meaningful connection.

observations.period: 2025 ATUS annual averages; care and household composition

denominator.unit: U.S. adults by presence and age of youngest household child; primary and secondary childcare measures

young_child_primary_care.unit: average hours per day of primary childcare among adults living with a child under age 6

young_child_gender_gap.value: 2.8 hours for women versus 1.7 hours for men among adults living with a child under age 6

young_child_nonemployed_gap.value: 3.3 hours among nonemployed adults versus 1.7 hours among employed adults for caring and helping household children

secondary_childcare.unit: average hours per day of secondary childcare among adults living with a child under age 13

mechanism.value: Care is woven into leisure and household activity rather than confined to a separately visible block of time, making the opportunity cost of family life easy to undercount

observations.method: BLS ATUS primary and secondary childcare estimates by household-child age, sex, and employment status.
observations.uncertainty: Secondary childcare is simultaneous with another primary activity; the estimates describe time allocation and do not identify causal effects on labor supply, wellbeing, or family outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Adults living with children under 6 or under 13, by sex and employment status.
observations.counterinterpretation: The same simultaneous care can reflect ordinary family co-presence and positive involvement, not only hidden burden; household support networks are not fully observed.

related_sources.claim: Complementary GAO valuation of unpaid household work using pooled 2021–2024 ATUS data.
BLS American Time Use Survey data, definitions, and historical series.

boundary: This record adds a U.S. time-allocation route from work location and education through unpaid household activity, childcare, socializing, television, computer leisure, and household composition. It is an annual cross-sectional time-diary release, not respondent-level longitudinal analysis, causal evidence, or a complete measure of simultaneous digital, care, emotional, or relational work.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official BLS ATUS 2025 results page reviewed for work location, household activity, leisure and socializing, computer use, childcare, subgroup comparisons, survey design, and the 2025 shutdown data-collection limitation.
